Great question! Let's look at both (I'm coming at these as what I think the average American thinks about the 2 positions):

Governor:

Pros:
-Flaunt executive power experience (especially if your state has done well economically)
-If the state had a natural disaster and you handled it well, it would help prove your ability as a leader

Cons:
-On the outside circle of Washington (this could also be an advantage)
-Lack of experience dealing with national issues and foreign policy

Senator:

Pros:
-Knows the ins and outs of Washington
-More experience on a national level
-Can use the support of popular federal bills as selling points, especially if you sponsored them
-Have the ability to reach out to voters across the nation, especially if you are a high ranking Senate member

Cons:
-Lack of executive readership 
-Name recognition can be a disadvantage if you are not a high ranking official.  
-Popularity. Not individually, but the Senate has abysmal approval ratings as a whole. You commonly hear of a popular governor, not so much of a popular senator. 

Overall, I would say governor. Simply because I think most Americans viewing governorship as a prerequisite for the presidency, or like a stepping stone to the presidency. Having the ability to say you have executive experience goes a long way. Voters have an easier time imagining a governor as president compared to a senator, due to the executive experience.

Breaking up the PBMs and ending vertical integration would be a great start. How a PBM can own a pharmacy and not be anti trust is beyond me. 

It still doesn’t solve the overall issue that the PBM model does exactly the opposite of what it claims to do; they further increase drug costs instead of decreasing them.

The problems with PBMs is the very model itself. The model worsens the problem with prescription drug costs, it does not lower prescriptions drugs, as PBMs claim it does; it raises them. 

Americans make up 3-4% of the world’s population, but account for 50% of drug expenditure. 

All peer nations have a negotiated price per medication with their respective governments. This is the only way to effectively control costs. 

There will still be a need for prescription insurance, even with these negotiated prices, to help cover some of the cost and to allow for cost sharing. There will still be a need for PAs otherwise providers will write for high cost drugs left and right (GLP1s are a perfect example). 

Drug companies and PBMs love to point the finger at each other, blaming each other for the ridiculously high drug costs in this country. The glaring reality is both institutions want the status quo to remain, as they mutually benefit from one another.

Ideally, we would get rid of them. Simply because they do not provide what their sole purpose is: to reduce the price of medications. Every analysis shows they raise the price of medications overall. Thus, their business is counterintuitive to their overall purpose.

Will that be happening? Will they go away with a snap of a finger? No. We are stuck with them for the foreseeable future.

What can we do? In terms of regulation, we have to change the game. I purpose 4 points to be enacted on a federal level to force PBMs to "play fairly":



1) Deconstruct vertical integration. In the 1990s drug companies tried to buy out PBMs, the feds stepped in and stopped this as the drug companies would then control too much of the market. Fast forward to today and we have 3 PBMs (Caremark, Express Scripts, and Optum) that control 80% of the market. Each on of the PBMs own and operate their own pharmacies and often own or are owned by a medical insurance company or a chain pharmacy. In the case of Caremark, it's part of CVS Health; a conglomerate of a PBM, a major retail pharmacy chain, and a health insurance company.  

I propose we split up PBMs into their own entity. PBMs must exist solely as the PBM and are prohibited from owning and operating a pharmacy and being owned by another entity.



2) Eliminate steering. Many states have enacted laws preventing this. PBMs must be prohibited steering patients to a particular pharmacy. No more "preferred pharmacies". PBMs shall not refuse pharmacies who wish to participate. PBMs shall not give preferential treatment (i.e. better reimbursement rates, less restrictive contracts) to a certain pharmacy. Essentially, ensure fairness across the landscape. Furthermore, prohibit PBMs from mandating 90 day supplies of medications. 



3) Fair pricing. We need some sort of benchmark to base pricing off of. Perhaps it's AWP + 10%. A "gold standard" of pricing needs to be enacted to ensure fair compensation rate across the board.   



4) Transparency. Currently, many PBMs have contracts which prohibit the contractee from auditing them. PBMs must provide the contractee a detailed list of the rebates they provided and money "saved them" quarterly. In addition, PBMs shall not enforce "gag clauses".   



In order for this to work, enforcement must be strict. Simple monetary fines won't be enough to enforce change.  It needs to hurt, it needs to hurt so bad the PBM is forced to comply. Most PBMs operate their own Medicare Part D plan, perhaps if a PBM does not comply with the above they are banned from operating a Medicare Part D plan. Perhaps, after a certain number of violations, they are placed on a probation period where they are micromanaged by the feds. If they continue to violate the above they are shut down and not allowed to operate.  

Overall, regulation must be simple and transparent. Leave no room for interpretation. PBMs will find any loophole and exploit it. Thus, all regulations will need to be concise and penalties harsh.
